reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Suspect scabies in any patient with severe, generalised itch that is characteristically worse at night
The pathognomonic lesion is the burrow, a fine serpiginous track most often found in finger webs, wrists, and other warm intertriginous sites
Typical distribution spares the head in adults but involves the face, scalp, palms, and soles in infants
Itch results from a delayed hypersensitivity reaction, so symptoms may take weeks to appear after first infestation but recur within days on re-infestation
It spreads by prolonged skin-to-skin contact, so all close contacts and household members should be treated simultaneously even if asymptomatic
Treatment is with a topical scabicide applied to the whole body per protocol, with laundering of clothing and bedding; oral therapy is useful for outbreaks or when topical treatment is impractical
Crusted (Norwegian) scabies presents with hyperkeratotic crusted plaques, carries an enormous mite burden, is highly contagious, and occurs in immunosuppressed or debilitated patients
Warn patients that itch can persist for weeks after successful eradication (post-scabetic itch) and does not necessarily indicate treatment failure
reference.pathophysiology: Scabies is caused by infestation with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. The fertilised female mite burrows into the stratum corneum, laying eggs and depositing faeces as she tunnels. The clinical eruption and intense pruritus are largely due to a delayed type IV hypersensitivity response to the mite, its eggs, and its excreta, which explains the delay in symptoms after primary infestation. In classic scabies the mite burden is low (typically a small number of adult mites), whereas in crusted scabies impaired immune control permits proliferation of thousands to millions of mites, producing thick hyperkeratotic crusts and extreme infectivity.
additionalDifferentials: Papular urticaria and insect bite reactions
Pruritus from systemic causes (renal, hepatic, haematological)
Bullous pemphigoid in older patients with intense itch
additionalInvestigations: Skin scraping of a burrow examined microscopically for mites, eggs, or faecal pellets
Dermoscopy to visualise the mite at the end of a burrow (delta-wing sign)
Clinical diagnosis supported by history of contacts with similar itch
Skin biopsy occasionally in crusted or atypical disease
Assessment for immunosuppression when crusted scabies is present
redFlags: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies with widespread hyperkeratosis and high transmission risk
Secondary bacterial infection with impetiginisation, and risk of post-streptococcal complications
Institutional or household outbreaks requiring public health and infection-control measures
Immunosuppression predisposing to severe or atypical infestation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent with correct treatment of the patient and all contacts; failures usually reflect incomplete application, missed contacts, or re-infestation rather than true drug resistance.
pitfalls: Treating the patient alone and not treating asymptomatic close contacts, leading to reinfestation
Incorrect application of the scabicide, missing sites such as under nails, genitalia, or the feet
Interpreting persistent post-scabetic itch as treatment failure and repeatedly re-treating
Missing crusted scabies in an immunosuppressed or institutionalised patient and allowing an outbreak
management: Treat with a topical scabicide such as permethrin applied to the whole body per protocol as first-line therapy
Use oral ivermectin for outbreaks, institutional settings, or when topical treatment is impractical
Manage crusted scabies with a combined topical scabicide and keratolytic plus repeated doses of oral ivermectin, with isolation given its extreme infectivity
Treat all household members and close skin-to-skin contacts simultaneously, even if asymptomatic
Decontaminate by hot-washing and drying clothing, bedding, and towels, or by sealing non-washable items away
Relieve persistent post-scabetic pruritus with emollients, topical corticosteroids, and antihistamines, explaining that itch can outlast successful treatment
Investigate for underlying immunosuppression, including HIV and HTLV-1, when crusted scabies is present
